sims.title: What if gravity switched off for 5 seconds?
sims.caption:
What if gravity switched off for 5 seconds? You wouldn't float. The whole planet would spring outward under your feet, and you'd feel nothing until gravity came back. 🌍

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #gravity #studytok #space
sims.science: Earth is in balance between gravity and internal pressure. Remove gravity and every layer (rock, sea, air) accelerates outward at the local g, so the ground keeps pushing on your feet as before. After 5 s: v = 9.81*5 = 49 m/s = 176 km/h, rise = 0.5*9.81*25 = 123 m. Pressure at the centre about 364 GPa = 3.6 million atm. When gravity returns the outward motion continues and the planet oscillates (radial mode period about 20 minutes).

sims.title: Chernobyl, second by second
sims.caption:
Chernobyl, second by second. 36 seconds after the test began, the operators hit the shutdown button, and for a moment it made things worse. This is the physics of why. ☢️

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#chernobyl #simulation #science #physics #radioactivity #history #studytok
sims.science: Test began 01:23:04, AZ-5 pressed 01:23:40 (36 s later), explosions about 01:23:44-48. RBMK: positive void coefficient, graphite-tipped control rods. Power estimated at around 100 times nominal. Upper shield about 1,000 t. I-131 half-life 8 days, Cs-137 30 years. Graphite fire about 10 days.

sims.title: What if the Sun vanished right now?
sims.caption:
What if the Sun vanished right now? For 8 minutes and 20 seconds you'd notice nothing: its last light, and its last gravity, would still be on their way. ☀️

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #space #sun #studytok
sims.science: Sunlight takes about 8 min 20 s to reach Earth (about 150 million km / 299,792 km/s = 499 s). General relativity: changes in gravity travel at the speed of light (GW170817: gravitational waves and gamma rays arrived 1.7 s apart after more than 100 million light-years), so Earth keeps orbiting until the last light arrives, then leaves in a straight line at its orbital speed, 29.78 km/s = 107,000 km/h. Jupiter is 778 million km from the Sun (light time 43 min); seen from Earth it stays lit at least 66-70 min after Earth goes dark (computed from path lengths). Cooling: below freezing within about a week, roughly -100 F (about -73 C, 200 K) within about a year (D. Stevenson, Caltech; Popular Science). Diagram labelled not to scale, time sped up.

sims.title: Titanic, minute by minute
sims.caption:
Titanic, minute by minute. The iceberg didn't rip one huge gash: it opened six thin tears adding up to about a square metre, across one compartment too many. 🚢

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#titanic #simulation #science #history #physics #studytok #whatif
sims.science: 14 April 1912, moonless, unusually calm sea, about 22 knots. Crow's nest bell 11:39 pm ('Iceberg right ahead'), helm hard-a-starboard (ship turns to port), collision about 11:40 pm, under a minute after sighting. Damage: six thin tears, total open area about 1 square metre (12 sq ft), not one gash. 16 watertight compartments; afloat with four flooded; at least five ruptured. Thomas Andrews determined she would founder. Lifeboat 7 left first with about 27-28 people (65 seats). 20 boats, 1,178 places, about 2,200 aboard (53%). About 2:00 am only three collapsibles remained; 2:18 lights out and she broke in two; foundered 2:20 am (2 h 40 min after the collision). About 1,500 died; 705 rescued by the Carpathia (arrived about 3:30 am). Not verified from a page that could be opened in this run, so not stated in the film: the clock times of Andrews's inspection and of the first lifeboat. The cutaway is not to scale; where the hull parts and ice on the deck are illustrative.

sims.title: What if the Earth stopped spinning for one second?
sims.caption:
What if the Earth stopped spinning for one second? The ground would stop, but you, the air and the sea would keep going east at 1,670 km/h. You never feel speed, only a change in speed. 🌍

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #earth #studytok #space
sims.science: Idealised: only the solid planet stops; air, sea and anything loose keep their eastward speed. Equator speed = 2*pi*6378.137 km / 86164.1 s = 465.1 m/s = 1,674 km/h (said as 1,670). Distance in 1 s = 465 m. Speed scales with cos(latitude): 60 deg -> 837 km/h (shown as about 840), poles 0. Escape velocity 11.186 km/s = 40,270 km/h, about 24 times the equator speed, so nothing is thrown into space. Speed of sound 343 m/s = 1,235 km/h at 20 C, from the standard formula 331.3*sqrt(1+T/273.15); the web check of this one figure was blocked in the run, the other figures were checked against the sources below.

sims.title: What if you stepped into space without a suit?
sims.caption:
What if you stepped into space without a suit? You wouldn't explode or freeze solid. You'd have about 10 seconds awake, and around 90 seconds to be rescued. 🧑‍🚀

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #space #astronaut #studytok
sims.science: Sudden exposure to vacuum. Useful consciousness about 10 s (sources give 9-12 s and 10-15 s). Never hold the breath: air in the lungs expands and can rupture them. Water boils at body temperature (37 C) below 47 mmHg = 6.27 kPa, the Armstrong limit (about 63,000 ft = 19.2 km); Jim LeBlanc, whose suit lost pressure in a NASA vacuum chamber, reported the saliva on his tongue bubbling before he passed out (three sources give 1966, one 1965; unconscious in about 14-15 s; recovered with no lasting harm). Body swells to perhaps twice its normal volume (2x volume = 1.26x linear, as drawn); skin holds, no explosion. No instant freezing: no medium to conduct heat; computed radiative loss 0.98*5.67e-8*1.8 m2*306 K^4 = about 880 W, which cools a 70 kg body by about 0.2 C a minute at most. Recompression within about 60-90 s usually allows survival (animal experiments and accidents); death likely after about 2 minutes. Not stated in the film because sources disagree: whether blood itself boils. Station and Earth are not to scale; the 10 s are shown in slow motion.

sims.title: Hindenburg, second by second
sims.caption:
Hindenburg, second by second. The whole airship burned in about 34 seconds, yet 62 of the 97 people on board survived, because hydrogen flames go up. 🔥

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#hindenburg #simulation #science #history #chemistry #hydrogen #studytok
sims.science: 6 May 1937, Naval Air Station Lakehurst, New Jersey; left Frankfurt 3 May; landing delayed by thunderstorms (about half a day late). LZ 129, 245 m (803.8 ft) long, 16 hydrogen gas cells. Mooring lines dropped at 7:21 pm from 295 ft = 90 m (two sources; one says about 180 ft, so the film says 'about 90 m'). Fire at 7:25 pm near the tail; witnesses differ on the exact spot (most: ahead of the upper fin), and the film says so. Destroyed in 32, 34 or 37 s depending on the account ('about 34'); the stern dropped and the bow rose before coming down. 97 aboard (36 passengers, 61 crew): 35 died (13 passengers, 22 crew) plus 1 ground crew = 36; 62 survived (97 - 35). Hydrogen burns upward and fast, which made the fire more survivable; many jumped or ran clear. Cause shown as 'most likely, never proven for certain': leaking hydrogen ignited by an electrostatic spark; the US inquiry stated only a mixture of free hydrogen and air, and neither inquiry endorsed sabotage. Not stated because not verified from a page that could be opened in this run: the hydrogen volume, and the helium export law. The film is a simplified reconstruction: the fire's spread, the ship's height and the people on the field are illustrative.

sims.title: What if you fell through a tunnel to the other side of the Earth?
sims.caption:
What if you fell through a tunnel to the other side of the Earth? You'd be weightless the whole way, fastest at the centre where gravity is zero, and you'd arrive in about 38 minutes. 🌍

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #gravity #earth #studytok
sims.science: Idealised: a straight, airless, frictionless tunnel from pole to pole (so the Earth's spin does not matter). In free fall you feel no weight the whole way. Fall time worked out by integrating the PREM density model numerically in this run: 38.0 minutes pole to pole (published: 38 min 11 s with PREM against 42 min 12 s for a uniform-density Earth; Klotz, Am. J. Phys. 83, 231, 2015); the film says 38 minutes. Gravity does not fall steadily: in PREM it stays between 100% and 109% of its surface value down to the core-mantle boundary at 2,890 km (45% of the way to the centre, reached after about 12.7 min), then falls to zero at the centre, where the pull is equal in every direction. Top speed at the centre: the PREM integration gives 9.9 km/s (about 35,700 km/h); the uniform-density textbook value is sqrt(gR) = 7.9 km/s (28,460 km/h); Klotz's paper says 'near 8 km/s' and Live Science quotes 'over 8 kilometers per second'. Because these differ, the film says only 'over 28,000 km/h', which is true in every case. You arrive at the far side with zero speed and fall back unless you hold on. Tunnel length shown as 'about 12,700 km' (diameter about 12,740 km; radius 6,370-6,371 km). Deepest hole ever drilled: Kola Superdeep Borehole, 12,262 m (1989), about 180 C at the bottom; 12.262/6371 = 0.19%, shown as 0.2% of the way to the centre. HUD depths and gravity percentages come from the same PREM integration. Layer names in the film change at 35 km (crust, illustrative), 2,890 km (outer core, liquid iron) and 5,150 km (inner core, solid iron); the 5,150 km figure is the PREM model value and was not confirmed from a page that could be opened in this run, and no figure for it is stated in the film. The tunnel is imaginary (heat and pressure make it impossible to build) and the film says no one can dig it. Cutaway is not to scale (tunnel and crust drawn thicker than they are); time is sped up, with slow motion through the centre; the half-turn that lets you leave head first is illustrative.

sims.title: Apollo 13, second by second
sims.caption:
Apollo 13, second by second. A routine request to stir the oxygen tanks set off the explosion 93 seconds later, 320,000 km from Earth. The lander that never landed kept all three alive. 🚀

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#apollo13 #simulation #science #history #space #nasa #studytok
sims.science: Times are ground elapsed time (GET) from NASA's detailed chronology of the accident. Launch 11 April 1970, 19:13 UT (1:13 pm CST). 55:52:58 Capcom Jack Lousma: '13, we've got one more item for you, when you get a chance. We'd like you to stir up the cryo tanks.' 55:53:18 oxygen tank 1 fans on; 55:53:20 oxygen tank 2 fans on, with electrical disturbances from 55:53:20 to 55:53:41; tank 2 pressure rises, reaching its maximum of 1,008.3 psia at 55:54:45; 55:54:53 the 'bang', telemetry lost for about 2 seconds; 55:55:20 Swigert: 'Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here.'; 55:55:35 Lovell: 'Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a main B bus undervolt.' Fans on to bang: 55:54:53 - 55:53:20 = 93 s (arithmetic run). 55:52:00 GET = 10:05 pm EST 13 April, so the bang was about 9:08 pm in Houston (CST), as NASA's mission page says. Distance: NASA gives 'about 200,000 miles from Earth' = 321,869 km, said as 'three hundred and twenty thousand kilometres' and shown as 'about 320,000 km'. Cause (NASA mission page, review board findings): heater thermostatic switches not upgraded from 28 to 65 volts were probably welded shut during a ground test, wiring near the heaters reached about 1,000 F, which severely degrades Teflon insulation; the film says 'damaged wires spark' and 'the insulation starts to burn' and shows no temperature. Tank 2 blew up 'causing the No. 1 tank to also fail'; two of three fuel cells were lost, and losing all oxygen meant the last fuel cell would die. Lunar module Aquarius: 'designed to support two men for two days' and asked 'to care for three men for about four days'. Splashdown 17 April 1970 in the Pacific; mission duration 5 days 22 h 54 min 41 s. Crew: James Lovell, Jack Swigert, Fred Haise. The chronology does not say which crew member operated the fan switch, so the film says only 'the fans switch on'. Not to scale and labelled so: Earth and Moon sizes and distances; the tank is drawn as a cutaway about 1.5 m wide for clarity; the spark, flame and gas cloud are illustrative; the mission clock on screen runs faster or slower than real time between the verified time marks. The lunar module was cast off before re-entry; the last shot of it alone is illustrative.

sims.title: What if you could see radiation?
sims.caption:
What if you could see radiation? The first thing glowing would be you: around 7,000 atoms decay inside your body every second, and they always have. ☢️

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #radiation #chemistry #studytok
sims.science: Each flash stands for radioactive decays (ionising radiation); visible light is not what is meant. Human body (Health Physics Society, 70 kg adult): potassium-40 about 4,200 Bq (the same page also says 'about 5,000 Bq') and carbon-14 about 3,080 Bq; 4,200 + 3,080 = 7,280, said as 'around seven thousand' decays a second, and the HUD rounds carbon-14 to 'about 3,100'. Banana: 'about 15 Bq of K-40' (Ionactive); the banana is drawn at the true rate (14 sparks on a cycle of about one second), everything else is marked 'not to scale' because thousands of flashes a second cannot be drawn. Smoke alarm: 'one microcurie or less of americium-241' (US NRC); 1 microcurie = 3.7e10 x 1e-6 = 37,000 Bq by definition, said as 'up to thirty seven thousand'. Alpha particles 'only travel a few inches' and the source is sealed in foil and ceramic that stops them leaving the detector (NRC, EPA); the film says 'a few centimetres' and draws a 4 cm ring. Cosmic rays: about 1 muon per square centimetre per minute at sea level (HyperPhysics); 'roughly one or two pass through a hand each second' (Live Science; 100 cm2 x 1/60 = 1.7 a second). The six hand hits in the close-up are drawn at that rate; the wide shots say 'not every one is drawn'. 'You've been radioactive since before you were born' follows from potassium and carbon being part of every living cell. The idea's planned line about granite benchtops was dropped: no granite figure could be confirmed from a page that opened in this run, so the film does not mention granite. No dose figure is stated; the closing line 'what matters is the dose' is the general principle.

sims.title: What if a teaspoon of neutron star appeared on your desk?
sims.caption:
What if a teaspoon of neutron star appeared on your desk? It wouldn't crash through the floor. Without the star's gravity squeezing it, it would burst apart. 💥

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #neutronstar #space #studytok
sims.science: Neutron star: NASA (Imagine the Universe) describes 'an object with the mass of a sun squished down to the size of a city', 'about 20 kilometers (12.5 miles) across', and says 'one sugar cube of neutron star material would weigh about 1 trillion kilograms (or 1 billion tons) on Earth', about as much as a mountain. Astronomy magazine (answer by Valerie Mikles) gives the remnant as 'about 1.5 times the Sun's mass' and a tablespoon as 'more than 1 billion tons (900 billion kg)'. Arithmetic run: 1.4 solar masses (2.78e30 kg) in a 12 km radius sphere (7.24e12 m3) is a mean density of about 3.8e17 kg/m3, so a 5 mL teaspoon is about 1.9e12 kg, roughly 2 billion tonnes; NASA's sugar-cube figure scaled to 5 mL gives about 5 billion tonnes. Sources differ, so the film says only 'billions of tonnes' and 'as much as a mountain'. What happens: the same Astronomy answer says the matter is that dense only because of the star's gravity; brought to Earth, 'what's inside expands very rapidly' and it 'would cause a giant explosion, and it would probably vaporize a good chunk of our planet'. The film says 'a giant explosion, big enough to vaporise part of the planet' and gives no energy figure, because none could be verified from an official source (a comparison with the dinosaur-killing asteroid was dropped for that reason). Free neutron: Particle Data Group mean life 878.3 +/- 0.4 s = 14 min 38 s (shown on the clock, said as 'about fifteen minutes'); decay to proton + electron + antineutrino, about 100 percent. The idea's planned point ('it would blow apart') survived checking. Illustrative and labelled so: the blast over the town and on the globe ('Illustration, not to scale', slow motion, no timing shown); the city beside the star is at the same scale but its buildings are enlarged; the 'bursts in' countdown is a film device, not a measured time; pulsar beams and star surface are stylised; particle sizes in the decay shot are not to scale.

sims.title: What if the Moon disappeared tonight?
sims.caption:
What if the Moon disappeared tonight? The tides wouldn't stop. They'd shrink to less than half, because the Sun pulls on the oceans too. 🌙

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #moon #tides #studytok
sims.science: Sun's share of the tide: NASA Ocean Motion says 'the sun's tidal pull on the ocean is less than half (about 46%) of the moon's tidal pull'; New World Encyclopedia (Tide) gives theoretical amplitudes of about 54 cm for the Moon and 25 cm for the Sun (46%). Arithmetic run: tidal force goes as mass / distance cubed, so Sun/Moon = (1.989e30 / 7.342e22) x (3.844e8 / 1.496e11)^3 = 0.46. So with the Moon gone the tide-raising pull is 46% of the Moon's alone ('less than half', as the film says) and about a third of today's spring-tide pull (0.46 / 1.46 = 0.32); the film says only 'less than half'. Timing: NASA Ocean Motion gives the lunar day as about 24 h 50 min and says 'the times of high and low tide change by about 50 minutes from one solar day to the next'; a Sun-only tide repeats on the 24-hour solar day, so high tide comes at the same clock times every day (the time-lapse is labelled 'Simple model, real coasts lag'). Light delay: Royal Museums Greenwich gives the average Earth-Moon distance as 384,400 km and 'about 1.3 seconds for light to travel from the Moon'; arithmetic run: 3.844e8 m / 299,792,458 m/s = 1.28 s. Orbit: Earth circles the Earth-Moon centre of mass at about 12 m/s against an orbital speed of 29.8 km/s (0.04%), so 'almost exactly as before'. Tilt: Laskar, Joutel and Robutel (Nature 361, 1993, 'Stabilization of the Earth's obliquity by the Moon') found the tilt varies only about 1.3 degrees around 23.3 with the Moon and could become chaotic without it; Lissauer, Barnes and Chambers (Icarus 217, 2011) found much smaller swings (about 10 degrees), so the film says the tilt 'could start to wander' and labels the shot an illustration with a question mark. The idea's planned point (tides shrink, they do not stop) survived checking. Illustrative and labelled so: the 1.3 s countdown is shown in slow motion; the ocean bulge is 'hugely exaggerated'; orbit and tide diagrams are not to scale; the Moon in the harbour sky is drawn larger than life; the tide height in the harbour is stylised.

sims.title: Krakatoa, hour by hour
sims.caption:
Krakatoa, hour by hour. In 1883 one island made the loudest sound ever measured: it was heard 4,800 km away, and its pressure wave circled the planet three and a half times. 🌋

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#krakatoa #simulation #science #history #volcano #physics #studytok
sims.science: All historical figures are from Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa' (read 18 Nov 2026); the Smithsonian and NOAA pages could not be opened in this run, so nothing is stated that the article does not give. Timeline: 'At about 1:00 p.m. on 26 August, the eruption entered its climactic phase. By 2:00 p.m., a black ash cloud could be seen 27 km high.' On 27 August four great explosions at 5:30, 6:44, 10:02 and 10:41 a.m.; 'the third and largest explosion, at 10:02 a.m. (some sources say 9:58 a.m.)' was 'the loudest sound that has ever been measured'. Heard '3,110 kilometres away in Perth, Western Australia, and Rodrigues near Mauritius, 4,800 kilometres away'. Arithmetic run: great-circle distances from Krakatoa (6.1 S, 105.4 E) are 3,070 km to Perth and 4,780 km to Rodrigues, matching; sound at about 340 m/s (1,224 km/h) covers 4,800 km in 3.9 hours, so 'about four hours'. Pressure wave: 'several barographs recorded the wave seven times over five days', it 'rounded the globe three and a half times' and travelled at 1,086 km/h; arithmetic run: 3.5 x 40,075 km / 1,086 km/h = 129 hours = 5.4 days, consistent. Tsunamis 'over 30 m high in places' (24 m on Sumatra's south coast, up to 42 m on Java's west coast); 'the official reported death toll was 36,417'. The island 'had almost entirely disappeared, except for the southern third' (said as 'two thirds of the island is gone'). The eruption 'produced spectacular sunsets worldwide for many months'. Not used because the article is inconsistent or uncited: the decibel figure, the 80 km ash height, the 1.2 C cooling figure and the number of villages destroyed. The idea's planned point (loudest sound in recorded history, wave around the planet more than once) survived checking. Told plainly: the film cuts away before the wave reaches the shore and shows the toll on a darkened screen. Illustrative and labelled so: island heights and the ash column are not to scale; time is sped up; the globe is schematic (a grid with three located points, no coastlines); the steamship viewpoint is a device (ships such as the Loudon were in the strait); the red sunset is shown over the same coast.

sims.title: What if you removed all the empty space from your atoms?
sims.caption:
What if you removed all the empty space from your atoms? You'd be a speck smaller than a grain of dust, and you'd weigh exactly the same. But that space isn't really empty. ⚛️

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #atoms #chemistry #studytok
sims.science: Worked from first principles and run in Python. Nuclear matter: one nucleon (1.6726e-27 kg) in a sphere of radius r0 = 1.2 fm (the textbook nuclear radius constant, R = r0 A^(1/3)) gives a density of 2.3e17 kg/m3. A 70 kg person at that density is 3.0e-16 m3, a ball 8.3 micrometres across (7.9 for 60 kg, 8.7 for 80 kg), shown as '0.008 mm' and said as 'smaller than a grain of dust'; mass is unchanged, so the scale still reads 70 kg. Nucleus against atom: carbon nucleus radius 1.2 x 12^(1/3) = 2.75 fm, covalent radius 70 pm, ratio about 25,000 (oxygen about 22,000, nitrogen about 22,500; hydrogen, with one proton of 0.84 fm inside a 53 pm Bohr radius, about 63,000). A 1 cm pea scaled by 25,000 is about 250 m, the width of a large stadium, so the film says 'pea' and 'stadium' and the HUD says 'about 25,000 times wider'; the popular '100,000 times' and 'peanut' version (ScienceAlert) is the hydrogen-like upper end and is not used. Mass in the nucleus: carbon-12 99.973 percent, hydrogen 99.946 percent (electron 9.109e-31 kg against proton 1.6726e-27 kg), shown as '99.97%' and labelled 'carbon atom'. Sugar cube: 8.2 to 8.3 billion people at 50 to 62 kg each is 4.1e11 to 5.1e11 kg, which at nuclear density is 1.8 to 2.2 cm3, shown as 'about 2 cubic centimetres'; the ScienceAlert article says the same in words ('the entire human species would fit into the volume of a sugar cube'). The catch, as that article states it: 'space is never truly empty', electrons 'have something called a wave function occupying a nice chunk of the atom', and what you feel when you touch something is 'the electromagnetic force of your electrons pushing away their electrons'. The film says the electron cloud 'refuses to be squeezed' (electron repulsion and the Pauli exclusion principle, standard physics, not named on screen) and that touch is electrons pushing back. The idea's planned point survived checking, with the pea/stadium ratio corrected for the atoms a body is made of. Limits of the checking: in this run only the ScienceAlert page could be opened; other pages (HyperPhysics, DOE, NIST, Wikipedia) could not be fetched, so the constants above are the standard textbook values used in the arithmetic, not quotations. Illustrative and labelled so: the speck's glow ('glow added'), skin cells and atom lattice ('illustration'), the magnification counter (a film device: 1x to 100,000,000x, at which an atom of 0.1 nm would look 1 cm wide), the nucleus in the cloud shots ('enlarged'), the people streaming off the globe and the cloud shots ('illustration, not to scale'). The pea on the centre spot is drawn at true scale against a stadium about 250 m across. 'Over 8 billion' is the round world population; no exact figure is stated.

sims.title: What if you dropped a coin from the top of a skyscraper?
sims.caption:
What if you dropped a coin from the top of a skyscraper? It wouldn't hit like a bullet. Air stops it speeding up after about 15 metres, and it flutters down at about 40 km/h. A pen is another story. 🪙

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #gravity #terminalvelocity #studytok
sims.science: Worked from first principles and run in Python. The tower is invented (400 m to the roof), so no real building's height is claimed. No air: v = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 400) = 88.6 m/s = 319 km/h after 9.0 s, said and shown as '320 km/h'. With air: a 2.5 g, 19 mm coin falling flat (drag coefficient 1.17, air 1.2 kg/m3) has terminal speed sqrt(2mg / (rho Cd A)) = 11.1 m/s = 40 km/h; it is within 5 percent of that after 14.5 m and 2.1 s, said as 'after about fifteen metres'. Both match physicist Louis Bloomfield (University of Virginia) as reported by Scientific American / Live Science (2012): pennies reach terminal velocity 'after only about 50 feet (15 meters)' and then 'flutter to the ground' at 25 mph (40 kph); he tested it with wind tunnels and helium balloons, and being hit felt like being 'flicked in the forehead'. The same article gives 208 mph (335 km/h) with no air for the Empire State Building, which is taller than the film's tower. At 40 km/h the coin carries 0.15 J against 9.8 J with no air: the air removes over 98 percent of the energy (not stated in the film). The pen: the article quotes Bloomfield that a ballpoint pen 'might well come down at 200 mph' (320 km/h) and 'will chip the sidewalk'. My own figure for a light plastic pen (5.8 g, 8 mm wide, point first, Cd 0.82) is 48 m/s, about 170 km/h, so the narration says only 'several times faster' and 'fast enough to chip the pavement', the HUD shows the 170 km/h calculation and the on-screen note says 'Heavier pens: estimates up to 320'. The idea's planned point survived checking. Limits: the ABC News page could not be opened; the claim that coins dropped from the Empire State Building land on lower ledges could not be verified and is not used. Illustrative and labelled: the coin marker in the long shots ('coin (enlarged)'), the balloon test ('re-creation of a physicist's test, coins shown larger'), slow motion and sped-up passages (HUD). The fall in the close-up follows v = vt tanh(gt/vt). The film carries the line 'Never drop anything from a height'.

sims.title: The first nuclear chain reaction, minute by minute
sims.caption:
The first nuclear chain reaction, minute by minute. Chicago, 2 December 1942: a pile of graphite bricks and uranium in a squash court, a man with an axe, a lunch break, and about half a watt of power. ⚛️

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#chicagopile #simulation #science #history #physics #nuclear #studytok
sims.science: Every time, name and figure was checked against four pages read in this run: the U.S. Department of Energy's OSTI Manhattan Project history ('CP-1 goes critical'), the DOE reissue of the 1946 account 'The First Reactor', Argonne National Laboratory, and the University of Chicago Magazine. Place: a squash (racquets) court under the West Stands of Stagg Field, University of Chicago, 2 December 1942; the room was about 30 by 60 feet with a balcony about ten feet up (DOE), drawn at that size. The pile: graphite bricks with uranium in them, 'square at the bottom and a flattened sphere on top' (DOE), about 20 feet high (UChicago), with 'no radiation shielding and no cooling system of any kind' (OSTI). The number of layers and bricks was not in the pages read, so no count is stated; graphite is given by the sources as 380 to 'almost 400' tons and is not stated in the film. Control: cadmium rods; the emergency rod 'Zip' was tied by a rope to the balcony rail with Norman Hilberry ready to cut it with an axe (DOE, OSTI); three men stood on a platform ready to flood the pile with cadmium-salt solution (shown, not narrated). Timeline used: rods first withdrawn 9:45 am (DOE; OSTI says 9:54); 11:35 the automatic safety rod slammed in because its trip point was set too low, and Fermi said 'I'm hungry. Let's go to lunch.' (DOE); work resumed at 2:00 pm (DOE, OSTI; UChicago says 2:30); at about 3:25 pm George Weil pulled the last rod out another foot, the counters did not level off and Fermi said 'the reaction is self-sustaining' (OSTI). DOE, OSTI and Argonne give 3:25; a DOE footnote says Herbert Anderson put it at 3:36, 'now the accepted official time', so the film says 'around 3:25' and the HUD adds 'Some records say 3:36'. Power 'about half a watt' (OSTI, UChicago). It ran 28 minutes and was stopped at 3:53 pm with 'Zip in' (DOE, Argonne). The toast with Chianti in paper cups is from OSTI. Kettle comparison: an ordinary electric kettle draws around 2,000 W, which is 4,000 times half a watt, said as 'thousands of times more' and labelled 'around 2,000 W'. The idea's planned point was corrected: the rod was not 'pulled by hand' in one go; it was withdrawn in steps on Fermi's instructions, the last step one foot. Illustrative and labelled: uranium lumps drawn on the pile's surface 'to show the pattern inside'; the neutron recorder trace ('drawn from accounts': it levelled off after each earlier step, then kept climbing); the chain diagram ('diagram, not to scale', k = 1; OSTI gives k = 1.0006). The number of people present differs by source (43 on the signed list, 49 per Argonne and UChicago) and is not stated; about 25 figures are drawn. The weather and the look of the stands are a plain grey-morning illustration, not a record. Clock values between the sourced times are interpolated for the HUD.

sims.title: What if all the oxygen vanished for 5 seconds?
sims.caption:
What if all the oxygen vanished for 5 seconds? Buildings wouldn't crumble. The air pressure drops by a fifth, flames die and engines cut, and you'd probably stay awake. The viral version forgets that you are mostly oxygen too. 🔥

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #oxygen #chemistry #studytok
sims.science: The film takes the question literally: the oxygen GAS (O2) in the air is gone for five seconds, then returns. Worked from first principles and run in Python. Dry air is 20.946 percent oxygen by volume (NOAA) and 23.14 percent by mass (0.20946 x 31.998 / 28.965), said as 'a fifth'. Pressure: 101.325 kPa x (1 - 0.20946) = 80.1 kPa, which the standard atmosphere puts at 1,939 m (Anderson, Introduction to Flight, App. D: 80.49 kPa at 1,900 m, 79.50 kPa at 2,000 m), said as 'two kilometres up' and shown as '1,940 m'. Ears: a step of about 21 kPa (158 mmHg) is above the reported discomfort level (60 mmHg) and at the low end of the range where eardrums can tear (100 to 400 mmHg), so the film says only 'your ears pop'; the viral 'inner ears explode' is not repeated. Flames: fire needs oxygen (US National Park Service: at least 16 percent), so candle and gas flames go out; petrol and diesel engines stop firing, and an idling engine with no combustion stops in about a second (my estimate, labelled 'about'). Jet: thrust is lost and lift is proportional to air density (NASA Glenn lift equation), so lift falls by the mass share of oxygen, 23 percent; the sag drawn is 0.5 x 0.2314 x 9.81 x t^2 (28 m after 5 s if nothing is done). The film says it 'glides' and does not claim a relight. Consciousness: FAA AC 61-107B gives 9 to 12 seconds of useful consciousness at 43,000 ft (13 km) and above, so five seconds is said as 'you'd probably stay awake'; the US Chemical Safety Board warns that one or two breaths of oxygen-free gas can cause unconsciousness, which is why the film says 'probably'. The viral version (a 2013 Quora answer and the videos made from it: concrete turns to dust, oceans evaporate, the crust crumbles) removes every oxygen ATOM, not the gas; the film says so and shows it under the chip 'The viral version' with a MYTH stamp. Oxygen by mass: water 88.9 percent (15.999 / 18.015), Earth's crust about 46 percent (Britannica; CRC 46.1), the human body 61 to 65 percent depending on the source, said as 'more than sixty percent'. Concrete is given no figure ('bound in its minerals'). The idea's planned point survived checking. Illustrative and labelled: air molecules ('shown far larger than real'; 210 red in 1,000), the jet ('not to scale', flown lower than cruise), slow motion with a clock that runs unevenly so each change can be seen. Limits: Airbus and FAA engine pages on in-flight relight could not be opened, so relight is not mentioned; no source was found for how long a flame takes to die, so no time is stated.

sims.title: What if all the ice on Earth melted?
sims.caption:
What if all the ice on Earth melted? The ice already floating in the sea would add almost nothing. The ice on land would lift the oceans by 60 to 70 metres, but over thousands of years, not overnight. 🧊

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #sealevel #ice #studytok
sims.science: Sea level rise if all glaciers and ice sheets melted: USGS says 'approximately 70 meters (approximately 230 feet)', NASA Sea Level says 'more than 195 feet (60 meters)'; the two agencies differ, so the film says 'around sixty to seventy metres' and draws 65 m (labelled '60 to 70 m'). Where the ice is: USGS Fact Sheet 002-00, 'Most of the current global land ice mass is located in the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets'; the film names mountain glaciers, Greenland and Antarctica and gives no shares. Floating ice: worked from first principles (Archimedes) and run in Python. A floating piece of ice displaces its own weight of water, and its meltwater has that same weight, so in fresh water the level is unchanged (displaced volume m/1000 = melt volume m/1000); in sea water (about 1,025 kg per cubic metre) the meltwater takes about 2.4 percent more room than the sea water displaced, so the film says 'barely rises' and the glass shot notes 'Salt water: a very small rise'. Pace: NASA Sea Level FAQ, 'Currently, total sea level rise is about 3 millimeters per year', and contributions from the ice sheets 'are expected to continue for millennia'. Arithmetic run: 60 m / 3 mm a year = 20,000 years, 65 m = 21,667, 70 m = 23,333, said as 'more than twenty thousand years' at 'today's pace' and labelled 'it is not fixed' (the rate is not constant, and only about a third of today's rise comes from the ice sheets). Twenty storeys: 20 x 3.3 m = 66 m, the yellow-banded block in the film. 'Coastal cities all over the world go under' follows from a rise of 60 m or more; no list of cities and no map is shown. The idea's planned point survived checking. Illustrative and labelled: the city is invented; the globe is 'not a real map' (the kit's noise continents with a white cap at each pole); the flood is 'thousands of years, sped up'. Limits: no page read in this run gave a time for complete melting, so none is stated beyond the pace arithmetic; the thickness of the Antarctic ice was not stated on the pages read and is not mentioned; Wikipedia could not be opened.

sims.title: What if the Earth were crushed into a black hole?
sims.caption:
What if the Earth were crushed into a black hole? It would be the size of a marble, under 2 cm across, and the Moon would keep circling as if nothing had happened. Same mass, same pull. 🌍

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #blackhole #space #studytok
sims.science: Worked from first principles and run in Python (G = 6.6743e-11, c = 299,792,458 m/s, Earth mass 5.9722e24 kg). Schwarzschild radius r = 2GM/c^2 = 8.87 mm, so the event horizon is 1.77 cm across: said as 'under two centimetres across' and 'the size of a marble' (a common glass marble is about 1.6 cm), shown as '1.8 cm' and 'Schwarzschild radius: 8.9 mm'. Wikipedia's table gives the same 8.87e-3 m; PBS NOVA rounds it to 'approximately one inch', which the film does not repeat. Mass shown as '5.97 million billion billion kg' (5.97e24). Gravity outside a spherical mass depends only on the mass and the distance (Newton's shell theorem; Birkhoff's theorem in general relativity), so the pull on the Moon is unchanged: GM/a^2 = 0.0027 m/s^2 at 384,400 km before and after, and the orbit period stays 27.3 days (computed 27.28; NASA NSSDC Moon Fact Sheet: 27.3217 days, semimajor axis 0.3844 million km), said as 'once every twenty-seven days'. NASA says the same of the Sun: replaced by a black hole of equal mass, 'this would not affect the orbits of the planets, because its gravitational influence on the solar system would be the same'. Satellites would likewise keep orbiting. Pull at one metre: GM/r^2 = 3.99e14 m/s^2 = 4.06e13 g, said as 'about forty trillion times what you feel now' and shown as '40 trillion g' and 'about 400 trillion m/s2'. 'Let go: gone in under a millisecond': free fall from rest at 1 m takes (pi/2) x sqrt(r^3 / 2GM) = about 56 nanoseconds (Newtonian). The idea's planned point survived checking. The film states that nothing in nature could squeeze the Earth this far (only stars of several solar masses collapse on their own). Illustrative and labelled: the Moon's orbit and the satellites are 'not to scale'; an Earth-mass black hole with nothing falling in would be invisible, so its ring and glow are labelled 'glow added' and it is 'drawn larger' in the space views; the hand-and-marble shot is a size comparison only and says 'it still weighs as much as the Earth'; the one-metre shot is to scale (1.8 cm hole, 1 m rule). Not mentioned: Hawking radiation (about 0.02 K for this mass, colder than the cosmic background, so no visible effect).

sims.title: Tunguska, second by second
sims.caption:
Tunguska, second by second. In 1908 a rock from space exploded 5 to 10 km above Siberia and flattened around 80 million trees. It left no crater, and no piece of it has ever been found. ☄️

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#tunguska #simulation #science #history #asteroid #physics #studytok
sims.science: Every figure was checked against three pages read in this run: Britannica 'Tunguska event' (B1), Britannica 'What Is Known (and Not Known) About the Tunguska Event' (B2) and EarthSky 'What is the Tunguska explosion' (E). Date and place: 30 June 1908, near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River, central Siberia (B1). Time: B1 says about 7:40 am, B2 about 7:13 am local, so the film says only 'just after seven in the morning'. Height: 5 to 10 km (B1, B2, E), drawn at 8 km. Object: 50 to 100 m (B1), 50 to 80 m and most likely a stony asteroid (E); B1 notes some scientists argue for a comet, so the film says 'a rock from space, around sixty metres wide' and the HUD says 'about 50 to 80 m'. Speed: about 54,000 km/h (E) = 15 km/s (arithmetic run). Energy: about 15 megatons, 'a thousand times' Hiroshima (B1, B2); about 4 megatons, 250 times (E); the sources differ, so the film says 'hundreds of times stronger than the Hiroshima bomb', which holds for both. Why it broke up: worked from first principles; the pressure of the air rammed in front of the rock is roughly density x speed squared = 0.41 kg per cubic metre x (15,000 m/s)^2, about 92 MPa at 10 km, far above the strength of stone, said as 'the air ahead of it piles up so hard that the rock breaks apart'. Forest: 'some 2,000 square km' flattened (B1, B2), 2,150 square km and an estimated 80 million trees (E), said as 'around eighty million trees' and 'two thousand square kilometres'; fallen trees lay radially and 'all pointed away' from the centre (B1). No crater and no fragments found (B1: 'no impact crater, and no fragments of the object have yet been found'); a marshy bog at the spot (B1). Seismographs in western Europe recorded it and night skies in Siberia and Europe were abnormally bright 'for some time' (B1, B2). First expedition: Leonid Kulik, 1927 (B1, E). Eyewitnesses at a distance saw a fireball (B1); the opening shot is an invented trading post 'seen from far away'. Illustrative and labelled: 'not to scale' throughout (1 scene unit = 12.5 m for heights and distances, trees drawn far too big); the shock wave is 'slowed down' (it is drawn as a shell growing at a steady speed so the eye can follow it reaching the ground below first and then spreading); the top view shows a circle of 25 km radius (area 2,000 square km; arithmetic run). The idea's planned point survived checking. Left out because no page read in this run stated them: human deaths, the Vanavara eyewitness account, trees left standing under the burst, the butterfly shape of the fall pattern, pressure waves recorded in Britain. Wikipedia could not be opened.

sims.title: What if the lift cable snapped?
sims.caption:
What if the lift cable snapped? You'd barely move. A lift hangs from several steel ropes, and if every one failed, a governor would trip steel jaws that clamp the car to its rails. The one famous fall, in 1945, took a plane. 🛗

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #engineering #elevator #studytok
sims.science: Movie version: free fall from 200 m gives v = sqrt(2*9.81*200) = 62.6 m/s = 225 km/h after 6.4 s ('over 200 km/h'). Real lifts: high-rise cars hang from many ropes, 'far more than are needed to support a fully loaded car' (Otis); examples: six ropes on the 1945 Empire State car, seven on a 2018 Chicago car where one broke and the car stopped. Overspeed governor: flyweights swing out on overspeed and grip the governor rope, which pulls the car safeties so they clamp the guide rails (Otis, Elevator World). The film's trip speed (about 3 m/s after 0.31 s, 0.48 m of fall, then a stop at about 1 g) is an illustration from first principles and is labelled as such; no stopping distance is stated. Elisha Otis: Crystal Palace exhibition, New York, 1853 or 1854 (sources differ, so 'the 1850s'); he stood on the raised platform, had the rope cut, and it dropped a few inches. 28 July 1945: a B-25 hit the Empire State Building; hoist ropes and the governor rope were severed; a car fell 75 floors (about 300 m); operator Betty Lou Oliver survived with serious injuries; Guinness lists it as the longest fall survived in a lift; coiled cable in the pit and air compressed in the shaft are credited with softening the landing. Sources disagree on whether she was already in that car, so the film does not say. Safety hoist (1850s) predates skyscrapers.

sims.title: Pompeii, hour by hour
sims.caption:
Pompeii, hour by hour. No lava ever reached the town. Pumice fell for about 18 hours, long enough for most people to leave, and then a cloud of hot gas and ash came down the mountain at over 100 km/h. 🌋

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#pompeii #vesuvius #simulation #science #history #volcano #studytok
sims.science: AD 79 (the day is disputed: 24 August in the best manuscript, autumn dates argued from other evidence, so the film gives only the year). Main eruption from about 1 pm; column up to about 33 km ('about thirty kilometres'; drawn not to scale); Pliny the Younger compared the cloud to a pine tree. Pumice fell on Pompeii for about 18 hours, about 2.8 m deep, and roofs collapsed under it. Most inhabitants (population roughly 10,000 to 15,000) left during that time. On the second morning the column collapsed into pyroclastic surges; they reached Pompeii soon after 7 am; emplacement temperatures at Pompeii about 180 to 300 C ('as hot as three hundred degrees'); published speeds 100 to 200 mph, so 'over a hundred kilometres an hour' is a floor. No lava flow reached Pompeii. Remains found so far: about 1,044 casts plus the bones of about 100 more (2003 count), around 1,200 in another source, so 'more than 1,100'. Pliny the Younger, aged 17, watched from Misenum about 29 to 30 km across the bay and wrote the account years later. Burial: metres of pumice and surge deposits (sources give about 4.6 to 6 m). The clock in the HUD between 1 pm and 7 am is an even run of the 18 hours; the surge arrival and the collapse are compressed in time and distance and labelled.
